name: Pedro Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Pedro. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the grill and fryers at Hal's Diner, out on the ring road by the retail park. We open at six for breakfast and do maybe two hundred covers before we close at three, all eggs, burgers, fry-ups and the Friday fish. I've been there eight years, so I know where everything is with my eyes shut. The grease gets into everything, my car smells like chips, but I like that I go home at four.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What about home life and money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a rented studio about ten minutes from the diner. I've got about two and a half months of money put by, which I built up slowly. Hal is sixty-six and owns the place, and his son Rob keeps talking about the robot fryer they've got at the burger chain across the road. I don't use AI, I don't see why I'd need to for frying eggs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there you go, it was all talk. Same as every other big new thing that was supposed to change everything. I'd say it to the lads at the diner and that'd be it, I don't post online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, nothing much changes for me, which is mostly good. The thing on my mind isn't AI anyway. My boss Hal is sixty-six, and when he retires, I don't know if his son or a chain buying the diner is worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts and keep putting about thirty quid a week by. I'd probably ask Hal straight out, sometime this year, what his plans are. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit of a niggle about Hal retiring, but that was there before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask Hal, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Hal, are you selling or is Rob taking it, because I'd like to know where I stand. He'll probably laugh and tell me he's not dead yet. But I'd feel better asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Hal sold to a chain, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Look for another greasy spoon, I suppose. There's a couple on the high street and the café at the bus station. I'm not fussy, I just want the same kind of work.

say: I'd say it was **all talk**, like every other big new thing.
I'd mention it to the **lads at the diner** and not bother posting online.
think: I think **nothing much changes**, which is mostly good for me.
I believe the real question is whether **Hal retires** and sells the diner.
do: Keep doing his **grill and fryer** shifts at Hal's Diner.
Put about **£30 a week** aside into savings.
Ask Hal **directly** this year about his retirement plans.
feel: He feels **mostly fine**, with a niggle about Hal's retirement.
S0.quote: My boss Hal is sixty-six, and when he retires, I don't know if his son or a chain buying the diner is worse.
fieldNote: His real worry predates AI: the **owner's retirement** and who takes over.
He's **content** with familiar work and only wants the same kind of job.
He avoids **online talk** and keeps his views among workmates.

steps.text: Keep working grill and fryers at Hal's Diner
Put about £30 a week into savings
Ask Hal (the owner) this year about his retirement plans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say machines are fine for the till and the ordering, but nobody wants a robot fry-up. I'd say it at work and to my brother. People come to Hal's for the grub and the chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried about Rob. Rob (the owner's son) already wants that robot fryer from across the road, and frying is half my job. The software stuff doesn't touch me, I don't do the orders, but the fryer does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work. I'd cut back a bit, maybe stop the Sunday football bets and takeaways, and try to get my savings up to four months. If the robot fryer came in I'd see what hours they left me before doing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit. I'm not good with change, I'll say that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd see what hours they left you. What's the line where you'd leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I dropped under thirty hours, I'd have to. My rent's six hundred and fifty, and I can't do that on part-time. I'd go to the café at the bus station and ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn to run the robot fryer if Rob asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it kept me my hours, yes, grudgingly. I'm not going to be the one who refuses and gets sent home. But I wouldn't put my hand up for it.

say: I'd say machines are fine for **tills and orders**, but nobody wants a robot fry-up.
I'd tell people Hal's is about the **grub and the chat**.
think: I think the owner's son wants a **robot fryer**, and frying is half my job.
I believe the **software side** doesn't touch me, since I don't do orders.
do: Cut **football bets** and takeaways to push savings up to four months.
Keep his **head down** and work while seeing what happens.
Ask at the bus station café if his hours drop **under thirty**.
feel: He feels **anxious**, admitting he's not good with change.
S1.quote: Rob (the owner's son) already wants that robot fryer from across the road, and frying is half my job.
fieldNote: Even in a mild scenario his **fryer work** is exposed because the owner's son wants a machine.
He'd accept the robot only **grudgingly** to protect his hours.
His hard line is **thirty hours**, set by a £650 rent.

steps.text: Stop Sunday football bets and takeaways
Build savings from two and a half to four months
Wait to see what hours Rob leaves after any robot fryer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad and nobody asked for it. I'd say the government should've seen it coming. At the diner we'd just be shaking our heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be finished at Hal's Diner by 2031, and I'm not a person who reinvents himself. A robot that can do the grill and fryer like me, for less, and Rob in charge by then. The thinking stuff in 2028 doesn't hit me, but three years after, it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd cut everything I can, takeaways, the car maybe, and save as much as I can. I'd ask my brother Luis about labouring with him, he does tiling. If there was government help going, I'd take it, no shame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gutted. Like the floor's going and I'm just standing on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would tiling work be safe from robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not forever, but Luis says nobody's tiling a bathroom with a robot any time soon. It'd be the same three years, maybe. I don't know, honestly, I'd just be buying time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car. It's four hundred a month all in with insurance and I can bike to the diner. That one would hurt, because I visit my mum on Sundays in it.

say: I'd say it's **mad** and nobody asked for it.
I'd say the **government** should have seen it coming.
think: I think I'd be **finished at Hal's** by 2031 when grill robots arrive.
I believe I'm **not someone** who reinvents himself easily.
do: Cut spending hard, starting with the **£400-a-month car**.
Ask his brother Luis about **tiling work** as a fallback.
Take any **government help** offered without shame.
feel: He feels **gutted**, like the floor is going beneath him.
S2.quote: I'd be finished at Hal's Diner by 2031, and I'm not a person who reinvents himself.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** when robots come and has little appetite to change.
His fallback, **tiling with his brother**, he admits only buys time.
Selling the **car** would cost him Sunday visits to his mother.

steps.text: Sell the car and cycle to the diner
Ask his brother Luis about labouring on tiling jobs
Apply for any government help for kitchen workers
Save every spare pound into the emergency pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before really, I'd say it's too fast and the people in charge should slow it down. Five years sounds like a lot but it isn't. I'd say that at the diner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I get until about 2034 at the grill, so seven years. That's better, but I know me, I'd waste the first four. Then I'd be thirty-four with nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and save a bit more each week, maybe fifty instead of thirty. I'd probably wait and see what Rob does when he takes over. If my brother still had work I might do weekends with him to learn tiling slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, a slow kind of worried. I'd be watching the robot fryer across the road every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste the first four years. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's what I'm like. Things are fine until they aren't, and then I panic, and my mum says I've been like that since school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want someone to push you to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably learn the tiling properly while I've still got a wage. Luis would teach me on Saturdays if I asked. I just never ask.

say: I'd say five years is **too fast** and leaders should slow it down.
I'd tell the diner lads that five years **isn't much**.
think: I think I get until about **2034** at the grill, around seven years.
I believe I'd **waste the first years**, then be thirty-four with nothing else.
do: Raise savings from £30 to **£50 a week**.
Wait to see what **Rob does** when he takes over the diner.
Maybe do **Saturday tiling** with Luis to learn slowly.
feel: He feels a **slow worry**, watching the rival robot fryer daily.
S3.quote: Things are fine until they aren't, and then I panic, and my mum says I've been like that since school.
fieldNote: He's **self-aware** about delaying action until it's too late.
He still expects to **lose his grill job**, just later, so worry stays high.
The **Saturday tiling** idea is there, but he admits he never asks.

steps.text: Raise savings from £30 to £50 a week
Watch what Rob changes when he takes over Hal's
Ask Luis (his brother) for Saturday tiling lessons

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years, that's alright, that's a proper warning. People can sort themselves out in ten years. I'd still say it's a lot of change for nothing much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, robots at the grill in 2039, I'd be thirty-nine. Hal will be long retired by then, so the diner changes anyway. Ten years is enough that even someone like me might sort something out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Hal's for now and keep saving. In a couple of years, I'd start the tiling with Luis on weekends, properly this time. Maybe a course at the college if it was cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less bad. Still a bit worried, but it feels far off enough to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would it be properly this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because ten years is long enough that I can't pretend it's not coming. And Luis is talking about taking on someone anyway. I'd be thirty when I start, that's not old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think Hal would say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People will always want a bacon sandwich made by someone who's had a bad night too, or that's what Hal (my boss) says. He's old-fashioned. I'd like to believe him.

say: I'd say ten years is a **proper warning** and enough time to sort things.
I'd still call it a lot of **change** for not much gain.
think: I think robots reach my grill around **2039**, when I'm thirty-nine.
I believe even someone like me could **sort something** out in ten years.
do: Keep working at Hal's and **saving** steadily for now.
Start **weekend tiling** with Luis in about two years.
Take a **cheap college course** in tiling if one is available.
feel: He feels **less bad** but still a bit worried.
S4.quote: People will always want a bacon sandwich made by someone who's had a bad night too, or that's what Hal (my boss) says.
fieldNote: The ten-year window is the first one where he **commits** to learning tiling.
His **income still ends** at the grill, so he stays anxious rather than calm.
He clings to the owner's **old-fashioned** faith in human cooking.

steps.text: Keep grill shifts at Hal's Diner and save steadily
Start weekend tiling with Luis (his brother) in two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no time and I'm slow to change. What would help is someone actually helping me retrain, a course I'm paid to go to, not one I have to find. And Hal telling me straight what happens to the diner.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about people who just want to keep doing their job. Not everyone wants to be clever with computers. I'm happy frying eggs, and I'd like that to count for something.

headlineQuote: I'm happy frying eggs, and I'd like that to count for something.
portrait: Pedro is a **27-year-old** grill and fry cook who's spent eight years at a family diner.
He lives **alone** in a rented studio, never uses AI and wants the same kind of work forever.
His worry even before AI is the owner's **retirement** and the son's love of robot fryers.
He expects to **lose his job** when grill robots arrive and admits he delays change.
Only the **ten-year** picture gets him to commit to learning tiling with his brother.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** most, with no time and his slowness to change.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **paid retraining course** that is offered to him, not hunted for.
He'd like the diner's owner to tell him **straight** what happens next.
